idiom_name: supplyAsync per recipient + allOf(...).orTimeout(budget) / anyOf(...) gather
implementation_notes: CompletableFuture is the standard fan-out: one supplyAsync per recipient on a bounded Executor, then allOf(...).join() to wait for every reply or anyOf(...) for the first completion, with orTimeout/completeOnTimeout supplying the deadline. The gap that matters is that timing out or cancelling the combination does not cancel the individual futures - orTimeout completes the combined future exceptionally while every recipient call keeps running - so partial results are read from the individual futures (isDone/getNow) and the stragglers must be cancelled by hand. Java 25's preview StructuredTaskScope is the structured alternative (third variant).
pitfalls: orTimeout/completeOnTimeout complete the combined future, not the per-recipient ones: without inspecting and cancelling the individual futures, the fan-out keeps consuming threads and connections after the caller gave up.
allOf carries no values and join() throws a CompletionException on the first failed recipient, hiding the successes; results must be read from the individual futures.
Using the common ForkJoinPool (no explicit executor) couples the fan-out to unrelated parallel-stream work and gives no bound on outbound calls.

variants.name: ExecutorService.invokeAll with a timeout (classic bulk gather)
variants.idiom_name: ExecutorService.invokeAll(tasks, timeout, unit) with cancellation of unfinished tasks
variants.implementation_notes: invokeAll(tasks, timeout, unit) is the pre-CompletableFuture scatter-gather in a single call: it executes the callables concurrently and, upon return, cancels the tasks that have not completed (JDK javadoc: 'Upon return, tasks that have not completed are cancelled'), handing back a list of futures that are either done or cancelled - a deadline-bounded gather including the reaping. invokeAny is the first-success policy (one result, the rest cancelled). It is coarse - one global timeout, no per-recipient timing metadata, input order rather than completion order - but it is the smallest correct realization when the caller is already synchronous and runs on its own pool.
pitfalls: A timed-out task and a task that failed both come back as futures; only isCancelled() distinguishes 'too slow' from 'threw'.
invokeAll blocks the calling thread until the timeout or until all tasks finished, so it must not run on a request-handling thread pool that the tasks themselves need.
The timeout is the only budget control: a per-recipient timeout has to be implemented inside the Callable, and the returned list is in input order, so reply latencies are not observable.

variants.name: StructuredTaskScope with a Joiner policy (Java 25 preview)
variants.implementation_notes: Java 25's preview StructuredTaskScope is the structured-concurrency form: scope.fork(...) per recipient and join() applying the Joiner policy - anySuccessfulResultOrThrow() returns the result of the first subtask to succeed and cancels the rest, allSuccessfulOrThrow() waits for all subtasks and yields them, awaitAll()/allUntil(predicate) cover the wait-for-N cases. The scope owns the subtasks' lifetime, so closing it cancels whatever is still running, and a timeout configured via Configuration.withTimeout makes join() throw StructuredTaskScope.TimeoutException. It requires --enable-preview, and the JDK 21-24 previews exposed ShutdownOnSuccess/ShutdownOnFailure policies instead of Joiners.
pitfalls: Preview API: --enable-preview is required and the policy surface changed between JDK 21 and 25 (ShutdownOnSuccess versus Joiner), so the JDK version must be pinned.
Subtasks run on virtual threads by default and only the owning thread may fork/join/close the scope: sharing a scope across threads is an error, not a pattern.
A timeout produces TimeoutException from join(); subtasks already completed are still retrievable from their Subtask handles, so a partial merge needs those handles kept.
